Downstream results

DIME in action

Facial landmarks, head pose, face parsing, and action-unit (AU) analysis on unconstrained video, all from one DIME encoder in a plain baseline setting: lightweight task heads, no specialized modules.

Panels, left to right: input · head pose · landmarks · face parsing · action units.

Key idea

Learning the variation within an identity

Faces share one canonical layout, so a masked autoencoder can fill in a plausible face from context while subtle changes vanish into the residual. DIME fixes the identity, recovers two mixed observations, and supervises how the recovered pair differs.

01 Pair by identity, so identity cancels

\(\mathbf{x}^{a}\)\(\mathbf{y}^{a}_{\ell}\)
\(\mathbf{x}^{b}\)\(\mathbf{y}^{b}_{\ell}\)
\(\mathbf{y}^{a}_{\ell}-\mathbf{y}^{b}_{\ell}=\textcolor{#b8541a}{\cancel{\textcolor{#9aa7b8}{(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s_a}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s_b})}}}+\textcolor{#355aa5}{(\mathbf{r}^{a}_{\ell}-\mathbf{r}^{b}_{\ell})}\)

identity term \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\): the person's average patch, → 0 when \(s_a=s_b\)
observation term \(\mathbf{r}\): what changed, and all that is left in \(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\ell}\)

Across people, a mouth shape may reflect who someone is or what they are doing. Within one person the identity baseline is shared, so it cancels in the difference. Identity labels only form pairs; they are never an input or a target.

02 Mix, mask, recover, without peeking

→ →

tokens of \(\mathbf{x}^{a}\)   tokens of \(\mathbf{x}^{b}\)  ·  one random 50% mask, applied in both orders

The two faces look alike, so copying the missing patch from the other one would be the easy way out. Source-isolated attention makes that impossible: every patch of \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{a}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{b}\) is predicted from its own visible half, by a decoder branch in which that patch was masked.

03 EDDS: align the direction of change

loss \(=1-\cos\theta_{\ell}\)length ignored

  • reversed
    change flipped
  • erased
    both recoveries equal
  • aligned
    smaller, same direction

Two reconstructions can each look right and still flatten or reverse a small change, paying almost nothing in RGB loss. EDDS compares the centered differences with a cosine, so only direction counts: a subtle change matters as much as a large one, and reproducing shared appearance alone cannot satisfy it.

The EDDS objective

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edds}}=\frac{1}{\max(1,|\Gamma|)}\sum_{\ell\in\Gamma}\bigl(1-\cos\theta_{\ell}\bigr)\]
\[\cos\theta_{\ell}=\frac{\langle\hat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\ell},\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\ell}\rangle_{F}}{\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\ell}\|_{F}\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\ell}\|_{F}+\varepsilon}\]
\[\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\ell}=\mathbf{H}_{P}\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\ell},\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\ell}=\mathbf{H}_{P}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\ell},\qquad \boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\ell}=\operatorname{reshape}_{P\times 3}\bigl(\mathbf{y}^{a}_{\ell}-\mathbf{y}^{b}_{\ell}\bigr),\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\ell}=\operatorname{reshape}_{P\times 3}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{a}_{\ell}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{b}_{\ell}\bigr)\]

Notation. \(\ell\) indexes the image patches, each with \(P\) pixels, so a patch is a \(P\times 3\) RGB matrix. \(\mathbf{y}^{a}_{\ell},\mathbf{y}^{b}_{\ell}\) are the raw pixels of patch \(\ell\) in the two observations; \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{a}_{\ell},\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{b}_{\ell}\) are the recovered patches, mapped from the decoder's normalized output back to raw pixels so that both faces are compared in the same space. \(\mathbf{H}_{P}=\mathbf{I}_{P}-\tfrac{1}{P}\mathbf{1}_{P}\mathbf{1}_{P}^{\top}\) subtracts each channel's spatial mean, so a uniform color offset is not counted as change. \(\theta_{\ell}\) is the angle between \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\ell}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\ell}\), the angle drawn in step 03; \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F}\) and \(\|\cdot\|_{F}\) are the Frobenius inner product and norm, \(\varepsilon\) a small stabilizer. \(\Gamma\) is the set of supervised patches: a fixed fraction with the largest \(\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\ell}\|_{F}\), chosen from the targets only; if the pair barely changes, \(\Gamma\) is empty and the term is zero, which \(\max(1,|\Gamma|)\) keeps well defined.

What follows. Because the loss only sees the difference \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\ell}\), the two recovered patches receive equal and opposite gradients, \(\nabla_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{a}_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edds}}=-\nabla_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{b}_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edds}}\): they are pushed apart along the true direction, and each update depends on the other face's current state. Since \(\mathbf{H}_{P}\) removes the mean, these gradients have zero mean per channel, \(\mathbf{1}_{P}^{\top}\nabla_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{i}_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edds}}=\mathbf{0}\), so EDDS never touches the constant appearance component; RGB reconstruction keeps anchoring what the face looks like and gradient orientation keeps local structure. Swapping \(a\) and \(b\) negates both \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\ell}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\ell}\) and leaves the loss unchanged, so no temporal order, reference expression, or identity code is needed. After pretraining only the encoder is kept: downstream inference takes a single image, with no pairs and no mask.

Brief abstract

Conventional large-scale visual pretraining shows diminishing returns on fine-grained facial tasks: learning more appearance does not necessarily improve sensitivity to expression, geometry, or local texture changes. DIME reframes masked autoencoding around two observations of the same person. Their shared identity provides a reference, while Explicit Differential Direction Supervision (EDDS) aligns the direction of change between the original and reconstructed pairs. Pretrained on the curated Face-20M dataset, DIME continues to improve as facial data grows to 20 million images, where a standard MAE objective begins to plateau. The resulting single-image encoder transfers across facial action-unit analysis, cross-domain anti-spoofing, facial geometry, parsing, and face generation.

Method

Same-identity pairs are mixed reciprocally at the patch level. A shared encoder with source-isolated attention and complementary decoder branches recovers both faces. RGB reconstruction, gradient-orientation recovery, and EDDS jointly preserve appearance, local structure, and inter-observation variation.

Results

On Face-20M, DIME-B keeps gaining from larger pretraining subsets while a matched MAE-B baseline changes little beyond approximately 6 million images. DIME is evaluated across seven task families.

Scaling with facial data

Emergent facial semantics

DIME as the latent space for face generation

Latent diffusion models do not generate pixels directly. An encoder first maps every training image into a latent space, the diffusion model learns to generate inside that space, and a decoder turns the result back into pixels. The encoder therefore decides what the generator can express at all. We plug DIME in as that encoder in two recent frameworks: RAEv2, which builds its generative latent space directly from a pretrained representation encoder, and REPA, which aligns the internal features of the diffusion model with the encoder's representation. Only the encoder changes; the diffusion architecture and the FFHQ training data are the same for every encoder compared in the table below: MAE, MixMAE, DINOv2, DINOv3, the face-pretrained MAE-Face, and DIME.

Why a representation encoder changes generation. Generic encoders organise their latent space around object semantics or, for face-pretrained MAE, around predictable identity appearance. DIME's pretraining is instead about how one face varies: expression, geometry, and local texture must be encoded because EDDS supervises them directly. The resulting latent space is face-focused and variation-aware, so the diffusion model finds coherent facial structure earlier, resolves fine detail sooner, and reaches a lower final FID. Relative to DINOv3-L at 100K steps, DIME-L lowers FID by 51.0% and 55.6% with RAEv2 and by 46.1% and 50.9% with REPA at 256 and 512 resolution. The space also scales better: moving from 256 to 512 output raises DIME-L's FID by only 0.47 with RAEv2 and 0.67 with REPA, far less than for the other encoders, and DIME-B already outperforms larger generic encoders. The generation results thus echo the pretraining motivation: representing variation, not just appearance, gives a richer and better-conditioned space to generate from.
